title: The Tuesday Account

scenes.title: The Offer
scenes.prose: The client chose the place: a hotel bar with too few people in it. Dana Keil had been out of the game two years, and it showed in the way she checked the exits twice. The client was a woman in her sixties, silver-haired, with the patience of someone who had never once been hurried. 'Two hundred thousand,' she said. 'In bearer bonds, sitting in a private vault in the Hartmann Building. I want them moved.' Dana turned her glass without drinking. 'I plan jobs,' she said. 'I don't run them. You would want that clear.' 'I want it clean,' the client said. 'Planned is clean.' Outside, the city ran wet and bright. Dana had promised herself she was finished with this — but she had promised herself a great many things, and kept fewer.

scenes.title: The Building
scenes.prose: The Hartmann Building was a tower of green glass on the financial mile, and Dana cased it for three days from a coffee shop across the street. The vault sat on the fourteenth floor, behind a law firm that rented the whole level and trusted its tenants. Deliveries came and went through a loading dock at the rear of the building, screened from the road by a brick wall and a single tired camera. A steady rain fell all three days, which suited her; nobody looks closely at anyone in the rain. By the third evening Dana had the shift changes, the camera arcs, and the slow, confident rhythm of a building that had never once been robbed. That last was the thing she liked least. Confidence like that was usually earned, and she did not yet know what had earned it.

scenes.title: Marco
scenes.prose: Marco Vey worked building security at the Hartmann, which was the entire reason there was a job at all. They met in a laundromat that smelled of hot lint and bleach. Marco was wiry and restless, and a faded tattoo of a swallow marked his right forearm; he kept touching it while he talked, the way other men check a watch. 'I have never worked with your driver,' he said, when Dana mentioned Sol. 'Whoever he is, that is your call and not mine.' He slid a cloned keycard across the folding table. 'Good for the tenant floors, not the vault — you will have the vault from the inside or not at all.' Dana pocketed it. Marco was nervous, and nervous was at least honest. It was the calm ones she had learned to worry about.

scenes.title: Sol
scenes.prose: Sol had driven for the crew eleven years and looked as though he had slept through most of them. He met Dana in a parking structure with the getaway car already chosen: a grey sedan, mid-range, three years old, the most forgettable thing on four wheels. 'It runs better than it looks,' Sol said, which is the most that can be asked of a car or a person. He was favouring his left wrist, sprained the week before in a way he would not explain. Sol and Marco went back further than Marco liked to admit — three jobs together, maybe four, in the years before Dana knew either of them. She filed that away. In her experience the things people left out of a story were the things that later mattered most.

scenes.title: The Schedule
scenes.prose: They set the job for Tuesday. Tuesday nights the Hartmann ran a skeleton guard, and the rotation left a four-minute gap when the lobby desk stood unwatched — long enough, if nobody's hands shook. Dana walked the crew through it twice in the safehouse, a bare rented apartment with a card table and three folding chairs. 'In and out inside the gap,' she said. 'If the gap closes, you walk away empty-handed. Nobody improvises, nobody is a hero.' Marco nodded too fast. Sol did not nod at all, which she preferred. A four-minute gap was not generous, but it was real, and a real gap beaten cleanly was worth more than a longer one earned by luck.

scenes.title: The Walk-through
scenes.prose: Marco took Dana through the building once, after hours, on his own pass. Dana was a planner, and a planner walks the ground when she can. The tenant floors were carpeted and identical, door after numbered door. The service stairwell ran beside the elevators, a grey concrete shaft with doors that locked behind you; she made Marco prop each one and timed the climb herself. 'You are thorough,' Marco said, half a complaint. 'I am alive,' Dana said. 'The two are related.' On the fourteenth floor she stood a long moment outside the law firm's glass doors, the vault somewhere beyond them in the dark, and felt the old pull she had spent two years pretending to be rid of.

scenes.title: A Loose Thread
scenes.prose: That night Dana could not sleep, and a sleepless planner is a dangerous thing. She laid the job out across the card table again and found the thread that had been snagging at her: the bonds were too easy, too clearly the thing she had been shown. 'The second drive is in the floor safe under the partner's desk,' she said aloud, to the empty room — and only when the words were out did she think to wonder how she knew it. She had been eighteen months out of the game; long enough to get rusty, not long enough to get stupid. Nobody on the crew had spoken one word about a second drive, or a floor safe, or a senior partner. Which meant somebody already knew — and somebody had decided she should not.

scenes.title: The Client Again
scenes.prose: The client wanted a final meeting, and this time she came to the safehouse herself, which Dana did not like at all. She was younger than Dana had remembered — barely forty, sharp-suited, her silver hair clearly a choice rather than an age. 'There has been a change,' the client said. 'The take is larger than I first told you. Half a million, not two hundred. I trust that is not a problem.' 'Changes are always a problem,' Dana said. 'The number is not. The change is.' The client smiled as though Dana had passed a test. When she had gone, Sol said the thing they were all holding: 'People who lie about small numbers lie about big ones.' Dana said nothing, because Sol had already said it correctly and there was no improving on it.

scenes.title: The Reveal
scenes.prose: Marco broke first, the night before the job, in the stairwell of his own building because he could not say it anywhere else. 'There is a second drive,' he said. 'A floor safe, under the senior partner's desk on the vault floor. The bonds were never the real job — the client wants what is on that drive.' He had known for weeks; he had been paid, separately, to keep it from the crew until the last hour, and the keeping had finally cost him more than the money was worth. Dana listened and did not tell him she had already named the safe aloud to an empty room three nights before. Some things you keep, even from a man unburdening himself — especially then.

scenes.title: The Night
scenes.prose: The job ran on Thursday night, because the client's drive could not wait for Tuesday, and money rewrites a schedule faster than sense ever does. The rain had finally stopped, the streets drying under a hard clear sky — bad for cover, good for nerves. Marco brought them in through the loading dock, and the dock faced the open street, not the rear of the building Dana had spent three days casing. His count was wrong from the first minute. The guard gap was not four minutes; it was ninety seconds, and Dana knew it the moment the lobby desk filled again behind them. They took the service stairwell — not the one beside the elevators but the narrow one at the far end of the corridor, the only door Marco's pass would open. The vault was not on the fourteenth floor at all; it was on the ninth, behind a law firm whose name was on no directory. Dana stood on the wrong floor in the wrong stairwell and understood, far too late, that the only person the plan had ever fitted was Marco.

scenes.title: The Drop
scenes.prose: They got out, which was more than Dana had let herself expect while standing in that wrong stairwell. Sol was waiting two streets over with the engine running — not the grey sedan they had agreed on but a black hatchback, swapped without a word to anyone, and Dana was too tired to ask whose idea it had been. Marco climbed in last. In the streetlight the swallow tattoo showed on his left forearm, dark against pale skin, and Dana looked at it a moment too long. 'Six years I have driven this crew,' Sol said, to nobody in particular, 'and that is the first time the plan itself was the trap.' Dana said nothing. She had the drive. She did not yet know whose side it would prove to be on — and that, she thought, was the only honest place to end a job like this one.
